question_text:
A 59-year-old patient with COPD is admitted with difficulty breathing and increased sputum production. Approx. a week ago, he developed an upper respiratory tract infection. On admission, his blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, the heart rate 92/min, the respiratory rate 24/min, the temperature 37.6°C (99.7°F), and SaO2 on room air 87%. Chest radiograph shows consolidation in the lower lobe of the right lung. Arterial blood gases (ABG) are taken and antibiotics are started. A nasal cannula provides 2L of oxygen to the patient. When the ABG results arrive, the patient’s SaO2 is 93%. The results are as follows:
pH 7.32
PaO2 63 mm Hg
PaCO2  57 mm Hg
HCO3- 24 mEq/L
What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 59-year-old patient with COPD is admitted with difficulty breathing and increased sputum production. Approx. a week ago, he developed an upper respiratory tract infection. On admission, his blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, the heart rate 92/min, the respiratory rate 24/min, the temperature 37.6°C (99.7°F), and SaO2 on room air 87%. Chest radiograph shows consolidation in the lower lobe of the right lung. Arterial blood gases (ABG) are taken and antibiotics are started. A nasal cannula provides 2L of oxygen to the patient. When the ABG results arrive, the patient’s SaO2 is 93%. The results are as follows:
pH 7.32
PaO2 63 mm Hg
PaCO2  57 mm Hg
HCO3- 24 mEq/L
What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Increase oxygen to SaO2 > 95%
opb. Re-take the ABG and observe the patient until the results are available
opc. Start non-invasive positive pressure ventilation
opd. Intubate and start invasive ventilation
ope. Administer oral corticosteroids

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient with COPD is experiencing respiratory distress, indicated by an elevated respiratory rate and low oxygen saturation (SaO2 87%). The ABG results show respiratory acidosis (pH 7.32, PaCO2 57 mm Hg), consistent with hypoventilation, which is common in COPD exacerbations. Given the patient's increased sputum production and consolidation on chest radiograph, pneumonia is likely contributing to his respiratory failure. The current oxygen therapy is insufficient, as evidenced by the low SaO2. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) is recommended in cases of acute respiratory failure due to COPD exacerbations, especially when there is hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2). Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is to start non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (option c). This aligns with consensus guidelines for managing acute exacerbations of COPD with respiratory acidosis and hypoxemia.
